evidence.claim: MVC participants experienced a statistically significant reduction in anxiety symptoms compared with waitlist control.
evidence.quote: At postintervention follow‑up, according to the adjusted comparisons, there were statistically significant between‑group reductions in depression scores (β=-2.21, P=.01) and anxiety scores (β=-4.82, P=.006)...

limitations: Only 159 participants provided post‑intervention data, limiting power for some outcomes.

The waitlist control may not control for placebo or attention effects.
Self‑reported measures could introduce response bias.

payload.context: University of Cambridge students aged 18+ without severe mental illness, 616 participants (309 MSS, 307 support as usual)

evidence.claim: MSS reduced psychological distress scores during the examination period compared with usual support, with an adjusted mean difference of -0.14 and a moderate effect size (β -0.44).
evidence.quote: MSS reduced distress scores during the examination period compared with support as usual, with mean CORE-OM scores of 0·87 (SD 0·50) in 237 MSS participants versus 1·11 (0·57) in 216 support as usual participants (adjusted mean difference -0·14, 95% CI -0·22 to -0·06; p=0·001), showing a moderate effect size (β -0·44, 95% CI -0·60 to -0·29; p<0·0001).

limitations: Only 74% completed CORE‑OM; 59% of MSS participants completed at least half of the course, limiting exposure assessment.
No control for non‑specific effects; participants and staff were aware of allocation, potentially biasing results.
Results based on self‑reported distress, not specific anxiety measures.
key_findings: MSS group had lower CORE‑OM scores (0.87 vs 1.11) with adjusted mean difference -0.14 (95% CI -0.22 to -0.06) and moderate effect size β -0.44 (95% CI -0.60 to -0.29).
57% of usual support participants had distress above clinical threshold vs 37% in MSS group.
Approximately six students needed to be offered MSS to prevent one from experiencing clinical levels of distress.
payload.methods_summary: Participants were randomly assigned 1:1 to an 8‑week mindfulness course (Mindfulness Skills for Students) plus usual mental health support or usual support alone. Outcomes were self‑reported psychological distress during the examination period measured with CORE‑OM, analysed by intention‑to‑treat.

payload.title: Do Mindfulness-Based Interventions Reduce Anxiety Symptoms in University Students?
payload.abstract: This review assesses whether mindfulness-based interventions (MBIs) reduce anxiety symptoms among university students, examining the magnitude of reduction, intervention formats, and potential demographic moderators. Evidence indicates that MBIs generally produce small to moderate reductions in anxiety symptoms compared to control groups [@P1][@P5][@P9]. Various formats such as web-based programs, yoga, and meditation are effective, though comparative evidence often shows no single format to be overwhelmingly superior [@P1][@P2][@P3]. Furthermore, demographic factors like gender and baseline anxiety generally do not significantly moderate these outcomes [@P1]. However, limitations include a reliance on abstract-only evidence for several studies and a weaker evidence base regarding specific comparative formats.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body_markdown: Anxiety is a prevalent mental health concern among university students, prompting widespread interest in non-pharmacological approaches such as mindfulness-based interventions (MBIs). This review synthesizes existing research to evaluate the overall impact of MBIs on anxiety symptoms in this population, focusing on the magnitude of effect, the efficacy of different intervention formats, and the influence of demographic moderators.

sections.heading: Magnitude of Anxiety Reduction
sections.body_markdown: Multiple systematic reviews and randomized controlled trials indicate that mindfulness-based interventions produce small to moderate reductions in anxiety symptoms among university students when compared to control groups [@P1][@P7]. Specifically, meta-analytic evidence reports moderate reductions in anxiety symptoms (Hedges' g = 0.46) [@P9]. Pragmatic trials evaluating programs like the Mindful Student Study (MSS) similarly demonstrate reduced psychological distress during high-stress periods with moderate effect sizes [@P5]. Web-based mindfulness virtual communities also yield statistically significant symptom reductions compared to waitlist controls [@P2].

sections.heading: Intervention Formats and Specificity
sections.body_markdown: Various delivery formats have been investigated, including web-based platforms, yoga and meditation programs, and brief mindfulness trainings [@P2][@P3][@P8]. While these diverse formats consistently help lower anxiety and stress [@P3][@P8], broad reviews often find no strong evidence that any specific format—such as traditional MBSR versus guided meditation—is universally superior [@P1]. Nevertheless, targeted enhancements like MBCT-TiF have shown benefits for specific graduate populations [@P6].

sections.heading: Demographic Moderators
sections.body_markdown: Understanding whether individual differences alter treatment efficacy is critical for targeted mental health delivery. Current evidence suggests that demographic factors such as gender, year of study, or baseline anxiety level do not significantly moderate the effectiveness of mindfulness-based interventions [@P1].

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.body_markdown: In conclusion, mindfulness-based interventions are effective tools for reducing anxiety symptoms among university students, showing small to moderate effect sizes across various delivery formats. Although demographic moderators do not heavily influence these outcomes, future research should continue to refine comparative format analyses using full-text data to strengthen the evidence base.
